'''''Senecio angulatus''''', also known as '''creeping groundsel'''<ref name="BI">{{cite book
 | last = Muyt
 | first = Adam
 | title = Bush invaders of south-east Australia: a guide to the identification and control of environmental weeds in south-east Australia
 | url = http://www.weedinfo.com.au/bk_bushi.html
 | access-date = 2008-03-31
 | year = 2001
 | publisher = R.G. and F.J. Richardson
 | isbn = 0-9587439-7-5
 | pages = 304 pages
}}</ref> 
and '''Cape ivy''',<ref name="CRC">{{cite book
 | last = Quattrocchi
 | first = Umberto 
 | title = CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=2ndDtX-RjYkC
 | year = 2000
 | access-date = 2008-04-14
 | publisher = [[CRC Press]]
 | isbn = 0-8493-2673-7
 | chapter = Page 2456
 | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=2ndDtX-RjYkC&pg=PA2456
}}</ref><ref>[http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_climbing_cape_ivy1 Cape ivy (mile a minute, climbing groundsel) (Senecio angulatus)] State of Victoria (Agriculture Victoria) 1996-2021</ref>
is a [[Succulent plant|succulent]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]] that is native to [[South Africa]]. Cape ivy is a scrambling<ref name="rbgsyd"/> herb that can become an [[Noxious weed|aggressive weed]] once established, making it an [[invasive species]].<ref name="NZP"/><ref name="nzpcn"/> It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] for its satiny foliage and sweet-scented flowers.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20170705011034/http://www.restoconlife.eu/en/creeping-groundsel/ Creeping groundsel]}} by Resto con life. Retrieved 15 December 2023.</ref><ref name="NZP"/><ref name="rbgsyd" /> 

It is a problem weed in [[New Zealand]],<ref name="gwrc">{{cite web|title=Cape ivy (''Senecio angulatus'') |work=Controlling problem weeds in riparian zones |publisher=Greater Wellington Regional Council |year=2004 |url=http://www.gw.govt.nz/story10945.cfm |accessdate=2008-03-31 |url-status= dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081015101701/http://gw.govt.nz/story10945.cfm |archivedate=October 15, 2008 }}</ref> and is [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in parts of [[North Africa]]<ref name="afpd">{{cite web |url= http://www.ville-ge.ch/cjb/bd/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=97995 |archive-url = https://archive.today/20130116074459/http://www.ville-ge.ch/cjb/bd/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=97995 |url-status=dead |archive-date = 2013-01-16 |title= Senecio angulatus L.f. record n° 97995 |accessdate = 2008-03-31 |work= African Flowering Plant Database}}</ref> and [[Southern Europe]].<ref name=genebank>[https://apg.pir.sa.gov.au/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=447151 Taxon:  Senecio angulatus L. f.] Australian Pastures Genebank Distribution Policy. Retrieved 15 December 2023.</ref> In Australia, ''[[Senecio tamoides]]'' is sometimes misapplied and is considered to be ''Senecio angulatus''.<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_angulatus.htm Senecio angulatus L. f.] by lucidcentral.org. Environmental Weeds of Australia. Retrieved March 25, 2025.</ref> Although it resembles ''S. tamoides'', [[Open Tree of Life]] indicates that it is most closely related to species in the genus [[Curio (plant)|''Curio'']], such as ''[[Curio articulatus]]'', followed by ''[[Delairea odorata]]''.<ref>{{cite web 
 |title=Curio / Senecio angulatus 
 |url=https://tree.opentreeoflife.org/opentree/opentree16.1@mrcaott76302ott691387/Curio--Senecio-angulatus 
 |website=Open Tree of Life 
 |publisher=Open Tree of Life Project 
 |access-date=2026-03-28 
}}</ref> Other common names include '''climbing groundsel''',<ref name="BI"/> '''angled senecio''',<ref>[https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/senecio_angulatus.htm Plants of South Eastern New South Wales] Lucid Central. Retrieved 12 April 2023.</ref> '''Algerian senecio''',<ref name = ncbi/> '''Jordanian senecio'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Murrell |first1=Z.E |title=Vascular Plant Taxonomy |date=2010 |publisher=Kendall Hunt Publishing Company}}</ref> and '''scrambling groundsel'''.<ref>[https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/senecio-angulatus Climbing groundsel Senecio angulatus] [[Brisbane City Council]], Weed Identification Tool. Retrieved 6 November 2022.</ref>

==Description==
===Leaves and stems===
[[File:Senecio_angulatus_006.jpg|thumb|200px|left|Leaves]]
Its form is a dense tangled [[shrub]] {{convert|2|m|ft}} to {{convert|6|m|ft}} tall<ref name="das">{{cite web
 | url = http://pebb.das.state.or.us/ODA/PLANT/WEEDS/docs/pdf/weed_card_vines.pdf
 | title = Kudzu ''Pueraria lobata''
 | access-date = 2008-03-31
 | author = Tom Forney, Steve Hurst
 | year = 2007
 | publisher = [[Government of Oregon]]
}}</ref> or a [[vine|climber]] that can reach {{convert|10|m|ft}} high,<ref>[https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/senecio_angulatus.htm#:~:text=Notes,margins%20few%2Dtoothed%20or%20entire. Plants of South Eastern New South Wales – Senecio angulatus] by  Betty Wood. Lucid Central. Retrieved April 6, 2025. Retrieved 12 April 2023.</ref> if suitable support is available. The stems are succulent, and are often [[variegated]] with pale yellow green and purple, which become woody as they age.<ref>[https://www.nrc.govt.nz/environment/weed-and-pest-control/pest-control-hub/?pwsystem=true&pwid=95 Cape ivy Asteraceae - Senecio angulatus] Northland Regional Council. Retrieved 12 April 2023.</ref> They are slightly angular (not upright) and usually sparingly branched.<ref name="NZP"/> Neither stems nor leaves are hairy.<ref name="NZP"/><ref name="rbgsyd">{{cite web
 | url = http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Senecio~angulatus
 | title = Senecio angulatus L.
 | access-date = 2008-03-31
 | author =  National Herbarium of New South Wales
 | work = New South Wales FloraOnline
 | publisher = [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney]]
}}</ref>

The alternate [[leaves]] are [[Rhombus|rhombic]] to ovate (diamond-shaped or egg-shaped),<ref>[https://www.frankston.vic.gov.au/files/assets/public/v/1/environment-and-waste/environment/biodiversity/pdf/invasive_species_guide.pdf Frankston City Council Invasive Species Guide] Frankston City Council. Retrieved 14 October 2023.</ref> {{convert|3 to 5|cm|in}} long and {{convert|1 to 5|cm|in}} wide and occur in 1–4 pairs. They are thick, glossy, fleshy and coarsely toothed, with one to three teeth each side<ref name="NZP"/> and bluntly lobed,<ref name="das"/> with upper leaves becoming smaller with fewer teeth or none at all.<ref name="NZP"/> They have a frosted look from a powdery coating on the lower side. [[Petiole (botany)|Leaf stalks]] are {{convert|1 to 4|cm|in}} long.<ref name="rbgsyd"/>

===Inflorescence===
[[File:Senecio angulatus flower racemes.jpg|200px|thumb|left|Inflorescence]]

''Senecio angulatus'' produces [[inflorescence|numerous flowers]] in open clusters at the end of its branches or stems.<ref name="NZP"/> The honey-scented flowers are on an elongated stem and open in succession from the base up as the stem continues to grow. The flower clusters are more flat at the top than pyramid-like, and are {{convert|4 to 8|cm|in}} in diameter.<ref name="rbgsyd"/>  Often the cluster droops with the flower heads at the end of the cluster turning upwards. [[Pedicel (botany)|Flower stalks]] are mostly hairless or with some short hairs, {{convert|6.5 to 10.5|mm|in}} long.<ref name="NZP"/>

Attached to flower stalks are 8–11 fine pointed [[bract]]s {{convert|5 to 6|mm|in}}<ref name="NZP"/> which are surrounded by 4–7 pale green and sometimes purple tinged  supplementary bracts at the base, {{convert|1.5 to 2.5|mm}} which make a cup shape around the base of the involucre. Individual flower-heads are radiate and urn-shaped.<ref name="rbgsyd"/> The corolla has a disc<ref name="NZP" /> comprising 10-15 dull golden yellow disc florets.<ref name="rbgsyd" /> Each disc floret is a hairless tube with a slight expansion below the middle and lobes {{convert|1.3 to 2|mm}} wide. 4-6 ray florets surround the disc florets and have yellow [[ligule]]s (that look like petals) {{convert|5.5 to 9.5|mm|in}} long that make the flowers look daisy-like.<ref name="das"/><ref name="NZP" /> 

An autumn-winter bloomer, the plant flowers from April to May in Southern Africa and May to July in Australia.<ref name="rbgsyd"/> In New Zealand, it blooms from March to August.<ref name="CABI">[https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.117058#:~:text=Senecio%20angulatus%20has%20moderately%20large,)%206%2D9%20mm%20long.&text=Delairea%20odorata%20has%20small%20bright,petals'%20(ray%20florets). Senecio angulatus] by  Julissa Rojas-Sandoval from [[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International]]. 30 May 2024. Retrieved 24 October 2024.</ref> In the northern hemisphere, it flowers from November to the end of January.<ref>[https://www.casaegiardino.it/giardinaggio/senecio-angulatus-senecio-rampicante.php Senecio angulatus – Senecio rampicante] by Laura Bennet from CASA E GIARDINO</ref><ref>[https://www.cosedicasa.com/casa-in-fiore/balcone-terrazzo/senecio-angulatus-il-rampicante-fiorito-a-novembre-91330 Senecio angulatus, il rampicante fiorito a novembre] by Giovanna Rio from Cose di Casa</ref> Under a full sun it can bloom in late spring as well, albeit sparingly.<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book,'' 1995:606–607</ref>

[[Achenes]] are {{convert|3 to 4|mm}} long,<ref name="NZP"/> ribbed or grooved with short hairs in the grooves<ref name="NZP"/> and a tapering cylindrical shape.<ref name="NZP"/><ref name="rbgsyd"/> The parachute-like hairs, the [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]], are {{convert|5 to 7|mm}} long.<ref name="NZP"/><ref name="rbgsyd"/>

== Cultivation ==
Due to its drought-tolerance and succulent nature,<ref>[https://landscapeplants.aub.edu.lb/Plants/GetPDF/dcc77b26-1656-4f5f-bbc3-a32e75aaa030 Senecio angulatus (Cape ivy, Climbing groundsel, Creeping groundsel)] AUB Landscape Plant Database. Retrieved 1 April 2023.</ref><ref>[https://www.nrc.govt.nz/environment/weed-and-pest-control/pest-control-hub/?pwsystem=true&pwid=95 Cape ivy] [[Northland Regional Council]]. Retrieved 1 April 2023.</ref> Cape ivy thrives in areas with a [[Mediterranean climate]],<ref>[http://www.consultaplantas.com/index.php/en/plants-from-s-to-z/2714-senecio-angulatus-or-creeping-groundsel-care-and-growing SENECIO ANGULATUS OR CREEPING GROUNDSEL {{!}} CARE AND GROWING] Consulta Plantas - Gardening and plant care since 2001. Retrieved 1 April 2023.</ref> where it has been cultivated in parts of [[North Africa]], [[Southern Europe]]<ref name="EUROMED">{{cite web
 | url = http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=7000627&PTRefFk=7000000
 | title = Details for: ''Senecio angulatus''
 | access-date = 2008-03-31
 | author = Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem
 | author-link = Botanical Garden in Berlin
 | work = Euro+Med PlantBase 
 | publisher = [[Free University of Berlin|Freie Universität Berlin]]
 }}</ref> and the [[Levant]]. 
===History===
[[File:Senecio angulatus bloom.jpg|thumb|250px|Grown towards a [[picket fence]] in [[Tel Aviv]]]] 
Cape ivy was introduced in [[Malta]] in the 15th century as an ornamental plant.<ref name="wildplants">[http://www.maltawildplants.com/ASTR/Senecio_angulatus.php Senecio angulatus (Creeping Groundsel)] MaltaWildPlants.com by Stephen Mifsud</ref> In [[Queensland]], the plant may have increased in popularity following the [[Boer War]], as there were anecdotal accounts that it was [[introduced species|introduced]] from South Africa by the soldiers who returned to Australia after 1902. Moreover, it was displayed in garden pillars in [[Brisbane]] newspapers between 1906 and 1910, praising the plant for the beauty of both its foliage and its yellow clusters of blooms. Though these reports may have falsely applied the ''S. angulatus'' name to ''[[Senecio mikanioides]]'', which was a weed at that time on the east coast.<ref name = "weeds">[https://weedsofmelbourne.org/climbing-groundsel-senecio-angulatus Climbing Groundsel (Senecio angulatus)] by Weeds of Melbourne,  July 10, 2019</ref>

It was most likely introduced to the [[United States]] after 1930, as it is not listed in the first edition of ''[[Hortus]]'', although it is rarely cultivated in that country.<ref name=aphis/> The plant was collected as a weed in [[Melbourne]]'s southern suburb of [[Mornington, Victoria|Mornington]] in 1936, and was displayed in newspaper column submissions in areas between [[Bendigo]] and [[Swan Hill]] in the 1940s and 1950s. In Melbourne metropolitan area, it became prevalent on [[Bank (geography)|coastal banks]] and on decomposed rock [[gullies]] of suburban creeks.<ref name = "weeds"/> It was introduced in New Zealand in 1940 as an ornamental.<ref name="nzpcn"/>

=== Propagation ===

Cape ivy grows in [[USDA hardiness zone]]s 9a through 11b, tolerating temperatures between {{convert|10|C|F}} and {{convert|38|C|F}},<ref name= "CABI"/> and is medium to fast-growing. Drought and heat tolerant, it would flourish better with some water in the summer and would bloom more often in full sun. It can grow indoors as a [[houseplant]], provided it gets some sunlight.<ref>[https://homeplantsguide.com/houseplants/senecio-angulatus-grow-and-care.html Scrambling Groundsel (Senecio angulatus) Indoor Care and Propagation Guide] homeplantsguide.com. Retrieved 25 October 2025.</ref>

[[Pruning]] is necessary as the plant can become limp when it gets taller.<ref>[https://weedsofmelbourne.org/climbing-groundsel-senecio-angulatus Climbing Groundsel (Senecio angulatus)] by Weeds of Melbourne, July 10, 2019</ref> [[Plant propagation|Propagation]] can be done by [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]] (as the plant easily roots from the branch tips). Seeds prefer consistent moisture and warm temperatures to [[germinate]]. Annual [[Fertilizer|fertilisation]] is necessary, though not mandatory. Pests include [[aphid]]s.<ref>[https://worldofsucculents.com/senecio-angulatus-climbing-groundsel-creeping-groundsel-cape-ivy/ Senecio angulatus (Climbing Groundsel)] by ''World of Succulents'', August 30, 2013</ref><ref>[https://www.esc.nsw.gov.au/living-in/natural-environment/introduced-plants-and-animals/weeds/weed-profiles/creeping-or-climbing-groundsel-senecio-angulatus Creeping or climbing groundsel (Senecio angulatus)] by [http://www.esc.nsw.gov.au Eurobodalla Shire Council]</ref>

==Distribution==
[[File:Range of Senecio angulatus-Current.svg|thumb|Distribution of the plant worldwide (2008)]]
[[File:Senecio angulatus, Israel.jpg|thumb|250px|Cultivated at an apartment complex in [[Jerusalem]]]]
Cape ivy is native to the [[Cape Province]] in South Africa, hence its name, where it is found scrambling over coastal brushwood and forest margins from [[East London, South Africa|East London]] to [[KwaZulu-Natal]].<ref>[https://www.smgrowers.com/gardens/vinesenang.asp#:~:text=San%20Marcos%20Growers%20%3ESenecio%20angulatus&text=This%20vining%20senecio%20comes%20from,plant%20remains%20in%20our%20garden. Senecio angulatus- Vining Senecio] San Marcos Growers. Retrieved 25 October 2025.</ref> Within South Africa, it is generally found in [[Drakensberg]] grassland, Eastern [[Fynbos]]-[[Renosterveld]], [[Southern Afrotemperate Forest]] and the [[Albany thickets]].<ref>[http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000058907 WFO (2025): Senecio angulatus L.f.] Published on the Internet. Access date 25 Oct 2025.</ref>

It has been naturalized in areas with the [[Mediterranean climate]], such as those in, or proximate to, the [[Mediterranean Basin]]: [[Southern Italy]] ([[Sardegna]], [[Sicilia]]), [[France]] ([[Corsica]]), [[Spain]] (including [[Balearic Islands]], [[Canary Islands]] and [[Madeira]]), [[Croatia]], [[Portugal]],<ref name=genebank/><ref name=aphis>[https://web.archive.org/web/20170221060840/https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant_health/plant_pest_info/weeds/downloads/wra/Senecio_angulatus_WRA.pdf Weed Risk Assessment for Senecio angulatus L. f. (Asteraceae) – Cape-ivy] [[United States Department of Agriculture]]. Retrieved 15 December 2023.</ref> [[Albania]], [[Tunisia]] and [[Algeria]].<ref>[http://www.herbmedit.org/flora/FL28_111-118.pdf Apparition de Senecio angulatus (Asteraceae) en Algérie] by M. D. Miara, L. Boutabia, S. Telaïlia & E. Vela,  3 September 2018. Retrieved 4 May 2020</ref><ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:243791-1 Senecio angulatus L.f.] by [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew]]. Retrieved 8 November 2024.</ref>  

Outside of the Mediterranean, it is found in some coastal areas in southeastern Australia (particularly the [[Mornington Peninsula]] in southern [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]]),<ref>[https://caws.org.nz/old-site/awc/1996/awc199614441.pdf EFFECTIVE CONTROL OF CREEPING GROUNDSEL (SENECIO ANGULATUS)] Peter M. Newton. Eleventh Australian Weeds Conference Proceedings. Dependable Services Pty. Ltd. Retrieved 21 December 2023.</ref> where it is spreading and listed as a significant environmental weed in Victoria.<ref name="rbgsyd"/> It is an emerging [[Adventive plant|alien species]] in [[South Australia]], [[Tasmania]], [[New South Wales]] ([[South Coast (New South Wales)|South Coast]]) and southern [[Western Australia]].<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/senecio_angulatus.htm Senecio angulatus L. f.] Environmental Weeds of Australia. Retrieved 30 September 2024.</ref><ref>[https://florabase.dbca.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/20665 Senecio angulatus L.f.] Western Australian Herbarium (1998–). Florabase—the Western Australian Flora. Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions. Retrieved 12 December 2023.</ref> It is reported to be invasive in [[New Zealand]], where it has been naturalized in the [[Marlborough District]] and [[Chatham Island]].<ref name="nzpcn">{{cite web|title=Senecio angulatus |publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/senecio-angulatus/ |access-date=2021-09-19}}</ref> In [[California]], Albania and [[Chile]], it is reported to be [[escaped plant|escaping]].<ref name=aphis/> In California, it has an irregular wildland distribution, mainly coastally from [[Santa Barbara, California|Santa Barbara]] to the [[Mexico–United States border|Mexico border]].<ref name=cal>[https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/risk/senecio-angulatus-risk/ Senecio angulatus Risk Assessment] California Invasive Plant Council. Retrieved 25 October 2025.</ref>

The plant prefers soils of black [[calcareous]] and grey [[sand]], sandy [[clay]] and [[limestone]], where it will be found in [[Coastal plain|coastal areas]] on [[cliff]] faces, [[mudflat]]s, wet depressions in [[dune]]s, around swamps, [[landfill]]s, [[scrubland]] and near settlements.<ref name="rbgsyd"/><ref name="NZP"/>

===Invasiveness===
[[File:Senecio angulatus on fence.jpg|thumb|250px|Naturalisation at a scrubland in [[Jordan]]]]
Cape ivy is easily dispersed by [[Seed dispersal|wind-blown seed]], stem fragments, [[Hemerochory|dumped garden waste]] and by the expansion of the plant through [[stolon|runners]].<ref name="das"/> It can become aggressive when it is established, where it may smother the existing [[Native plant|native vegetation]] both in the ground layer and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]], thus altering the light climate in the invaded community and sometimes suppress the [[Regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] of native plants.<ref name="das"/> As such, the plant is targeted by the [[Oregon Department of Agriculture]] for early detection and fast response if it were to escape from cultivation.<ref name=aphis/> 

On the [[Costa Brava]] in Spain, it was one of the five most recorded species, where it was found in large assemblage, usually close to human residence, invading and colonizing the clifftops, roadsides and the proximate [[scrubland]], including the undergrowth, replacing native flora species such as ''[[Pistacia lentiscus]]''. It was introduced to [[Catalonia]] in the 1970s as a [[groundcover]] plant in home gardens, before escaping. Although it is not recorded as an invasive species in the ''Spanish Catalogue of Invasive Species'', it is one of the most common alien species present on the Catalan coast as it clearly possesses invasive behaviour.<ref>[https://lifemedcliffs.org/en/featured-plant-senecio-angulatus/ THE FEATURED PLANT – Senecio angulatus] LIFE medCLIFFS. 7 February 2023. Retrieved 14 October 2023.</ref>

It is described as one of the most invasive species in the western Mediterranean area (Brundu et al., 1999) and a major invader in [[Southern France|Mediterranean France]].<ref name=cal/>

==Chemistry==
Seeds are reported to be unviable and that the predominate mode of dispersal is [[vegetative reproduction]]. In a 2001 [[Wellington]] study, artificially pollinated [[Stigma (botany)|stigmata]] varnished with [[aniline]] blue under a [[Ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy|UV microscope]] displayed that a low number of [[pollen grain]]s corresponded to the stigmatic surface.<ref name= "CABI"/> [[Callose]] occurred in the few pollen tubes that did adhere to the surface, hinting the presence of a [[sporophytic]] [[self-incompatibility]] mechanism, which aids the theory that ''S. angulatus'' and ''Delairea odorata'' consist of a single [[genotype]] (or are set for a single S [[allele]]), thus seed is incapable of being produced.<ref name= "CABI"/><ref>[https://envirolink.govt.nz/assets/Envirolink/225NLRC29.pdf Options for restoration of Cape ivy (Senecio angulatus)] – dominated sites using native coastal species, [[Glinks Gully]], Northland David Bergin, Envirolink, 2006  </ref>

===Medicinal===
[[Phytochemical]] profiling showed [[antioxidant]] and anti-[[acetylcholinesterase]] activities in extracts from Algerian ''Senecio angulatus''. The hydro-[[methanolic]] and the [[acetate]] extracts have exhibited  antioxidant potential of acetate for [[Ferric reducing ability of plasma|FRAP]] and [[phenanthroline]] methods. Furthermore, a high amount of [[cynarin]] and trans-[[ferulic]] acid was found in the extract whereas [[butanolic]] infusion had recorded the highest amount of [[chlorogenic acid]]. Though [[Phenols|phenolic]] compounds tend to have [[hydroxyl]] in their composition, contributing to the antioxidant activity.<ref name = ncbi>[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34219549/ LC-ESI/MS-phytochemical profiling with antioxidant and antiacetylcholinesterase activities of Algerian Senecio angulatus L.f. extracts] Ahlem Bousetla, Hatice Banu Keskinkaya, Chawki Bensouici, Mostefa Lefahal, Mehmet Nuri Atalar, Salah Akkal. [[National Library of Medicine]]. 21 July 2021.</ref>
